title: Self-Paced Module: HTML Fundamentals, Paragraphs and Lists

lessons.title: Meet HTML: Juan Dela Cruz's First Resume Page

objectives.cognitive: Explain the role and versions of HTML and the parts of a page: doctype, html, head, title, body, elements, attributes and values.
objectives.affective: Show care for privacy by putting only safe, made-up details on a sample resume page.
objectives.psychomotor: Run Juan's first resume page in CodeShare's code editor and add a paragraph to its body.

blocks.markdown: **How to use this module:** Work in order, Monday to Friday. Every step has three parts: run the sample unchanged and read its discussion, type the guided example and run it, then do Your task on your own. The guided example never completes a step; only Your task does. Answer each day's exit slip after its last step.

**Everything happens in CodeShare.** Open your class, then **Module**, this week and a step. **Work in code editor** loads the step's sample into index.html; **Run code** shows the page in the page window and checks it. It works online and from the classroom laptop; no internet, installation, download or account is needed.

**Reading the outputs:** an output box shows the page text CodeShare checks: the Tab title, then the Visible page text. List numbers and bullets, bold and highlights are drawn on the page but are not page text; page checks look at them instead. Spaces count.
**Where we start:** This is the first week, so your module project starts empty. Step 1 creates index.html; every later step grows the same page.
**Week 1 starts here:** Plain words with no HTML run together: a name, an introduction and skills typed in body appear on one line.

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) gives a web page its meaning and structure: headings, paragraphs and lists. CSS, from Week 4, changes how it looks. A web editor is where you write HTML; in this course it is CodeShare's code editor, and Run code shows the page in the page window.
A printed resume has a name at the top, a short introduction and lists. HTML labels each part so the browser, and a screen reader, know which part is which.

rows: The first HTML; many revisions and additions in its first five years.
HTML 3.2, then HTML4 the same year (W3C).
XHTML 1.0: HTML4 rewritten in the stricter XML style.
Work on HTML5 begins, led by browser makers (WHATWG).
W3C and WHATWG agree on one HTML: the HTML Living Standard. The doctype line means today's HTML.

blocks.markdown: **Syntax:** an element is an opening tag, its content and a closing tag. An attribute such as lang="en" sits in the opening tag; "en" is its value. Elements nest: the inner one closes first. br and hr have no closing tag.

lessons.title: Format Juan's Introduction: Paragraph Formatting Elements

objectives.cognitive: Explain how b, strong, i, em, mark, small, sub, sup, br, hr and pre change a page and its page text.
objectives.affective: Value clear and honest wording when describing one's own skills.
objectives.psychomotor: Format Juan's introduction, motto and club schedule, then add one formatted line.

blocks.markdown: **Today's starting point:** Monday's page cannot keep a line break or extra spaces: a three-line motto and a lined-up schedule run together.

Inside a paragraph, strong marks important words and em stresses words; b and i set words apart without extra importance; mark highlights; small is for side comments; sub and sup lower or raise characters. br breaks a line, hr marks a change of topic, and pre keeps spaces and line breaks exactly as typed.
A teacher's red pen marks what matters in an essay without changing the words. Formatting elements mark words the same way.

blocks.instruction: Juan's introduction gets more formatting: sup, sub, b, i, mark and small. Run the sample unchanged, then find the words of each element in the output.

lessons.title: List Juan's Skills and Interests: List Attributes and Values

objectives.cognitive: Explain unordered and ordered lists and the type, start and reversed attributes and their values.
objectives.affective: Organise information so that classmates and future employers can read it quickly.
objectives.psychomotor: Build Juan's skills, interests and goals lists, including a list inside a list.

blocks.markdown: **Today's starting point:** Juan's interests written in one paragraph with commas are hard to scan, and Monday's goals list is only numbers.

ul groups items whose order does not matter (bullets); ol groups items whose order matters (numbers or letters). Each item is an li. On ol, type picks the markers (1, A, a, I, i), start picks the first number (always a whole number) and reversed counts down. A list can sit inside an li.
A jeepney signboard lists its stops in order: that is an ol. A sari-sari store sign lists what it sells in any order: that is a ul.

rows: 1 (numbers, the default), A, a, I, i
A whole number, even with letters

performanceTask.title: My Resume, Week 1: Personal Info Page
performanceTask.markdown:
Start Thursday; finish and present Friday. In CodeShare open Projects, then Personal performance-task project. Your own resume starts there; it carries forward every week until Week 10.

Build a simple personal info page about yourself: your name as the main heading, a short introduction paragraph, and lists of your skills and interests. Use only safe details: your name, school, strand, skills, interests and achievements. Never put your home address, phone number, birth date, ID numbers or personal social-media accounts on the page.

Use this week's HTML: at least two paragraph formatting elements, a br or an hr, a bullet list and one numbered list that uses type, start or reversed. Run code until the page runs with no error, then press Submit this version. Saving or running is not submitting.

Thursday: 0–60 minutes, repairs and the Thursday strip; 60–120 minutes, plan on paper, show the teacher, then start. Friday: 0–30 minutes, finish and run; 30–105 minutes, five-minute presentations; 105–120 minutes, Friday strip and Submit this version.
checklist: Keep the doctype, html lang="en", head with meta charset and your own title, and body.
Put your name in one h1.
Write a short introduction paragraph about yourself (safe details only).
Use at least two formatting elements for their meaning, such as strong, em, mark or small.
Use a br inside a paragraph or an hr between two topics.
List at least three skills in a ul.
Add one ol (for example, your goals) that uses type, start or reversed.
No home address, phone number, birth date, ID numbers or social-media accounts.
Run code shows no error; press Submit this version, then present.
